conceptTag: The cost to win a customer
readerTitle: The trade show that looked like a bargain
caseNote: 가상 사례 (포장 박스 제조사, 업무용 소프트웨어) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 고객 한 명을 얻는 비용은 광고비가 아니라, 그 고객을 얻으려고 쓴 모든 돈(영업 인력의 시간, 샘플, 출장, 가입 혜택)을 새로 얻은 고객 수로 나눈 값이다.
misconception: 고객 획득 비용은 광고비나 행사비를 새 고객 수로 나누면 된다. 눈에 보이는 청구서가 곧 비용이다.

sources.text: 마케팅·관리회계의 표준 개념 (고객 획득 비용, CAC)

cards.title: The trade show that looked like a bargain
body: A packaging maker spends $12,000 on a booth at an industry trade show. Twenty-four new business customers sign up afterward.
That's $500 a customer. The online ads, by comparison, cost $1,200 a customer. Easy decision. Except it was the wrong one.

image.label: Trade show booth stacked with cardboard boxes
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 산업 전시회의 작은 부스에 골판지 박스가 쌓여 있고, 부스 앞에 "$500 per customer?"라는 말풍선. 부스 뒤 그림자 속에 출장 가방, 샘플 상자, 시계가 희미하게 숨어 있음. 실제 기업 로고 사용 금지.

cards.title: Which channel wins customers more cheaply?
body: Last quarter, the trade show booth cost $12,000 and brought 24 new customers. Online ads cost $18,000 and brought 15.
Next year's budget can only fund one. Which do you keep?

options.text: The trade show. $500 a customer beats $1,200
options.feedback: It uses the only numbers on the invoices. But the booth wasn't the only thing the trade show cost.

options.text: The ads. Online is usually cheaper
options.feedback: It may turn out right, but for the wrong reason. A rule of thumb can't replace your own numbers.

options.text: Neither yet. First add every other cost each channel needed
options.feedback: Right. Travel, samples and sales time are part of what each customer cost. The next card adds them up.

cards.title: What the trade show really cost.
body: Two sales reps spent half their time for three months following up with booth visitors. Divided by 24 customers, that's about **$1,917** each, not $500.

breakdown.label: Booth and fees
breakdown.detail: The only invoice anyone looked at

breakdown.label: Travel and hotel
breakdown.detail: Flights, rooms, meals for the team

breakdown.label: Samples
breakdown.detail: Boxes made and shipped to prospects

cards.title: The cheap channel was the expensive one.
body: The ads needed little extra: $1,000 in samples and $2,000 of sales calls. That's $21,000 for 15 customers, or $1,400 each.
Counting everything, the ads won customers about 27% more cheaply.

image.label: Booth sticker vs fully loaded CAC

cards.title: Customer acquisition cost
body: **Customer acquisition cost**, often shortened to CAC, is everything you spent to win new customers in a period, divided by the number of new customers you won.
The key word is *everything*. Invoices are easy to see. People's time, free samples and sign-up deals are easy to miss. The missing part is often the biggest part.

image.label: Iceberg: ad spend above water, other costs below
image.brief: 빙산 일러스트. 물 위의 작은 부분에 "Ads / Booth", 물 아래의 큰 부분에 "Sales time", "Samples", "Travel", "Sign-up discounts", "Tools" 라벨. 차분한 파란 톤.

cards.title: What goes into the cost to win a customer.
body: Ask one question of every cost: would we have spent this if we weren't trying to win new customers?
list: **Paid reach:** ads, events, listings, printed materials
**People:** time sales and marketing staff spend on new customers, plus commissions
**Tools:** software and agencies used to find and sign customers
cards.callout: Leave out the cost of serving customers you already have. That belongs elsewhere.

cards.title: The number is only as honest as its parts.
body: Splitting a salesperson's time is an estimate. Make a reasonable split and use it every time, so channels stay comparable.
Timing can mislead too. Money spent this quarter may win customers next quarter. And customers who would have come anyway, like referrals, shouldn't make a paid channel look cheap.
Finally, a low cost isn't good on its own. It depends on what a customer is worth, which is the next lesson.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your team-scheduling app spent $20,000 on ads last month. Two salespeople spent $12,000 worth of time running demos. Every new customer got the first month free, a $10 value.
1,200 people started a free trial. 400 became paying customers. What did each customer cost?

options.text: $30: total cost divided by 1,200 trial sign-ups
options.feedback: Trial users haven't paid. Counting them makes the cost look a third of what it is.

options.text: $50: ad spend divided by 400 paying customers
options.feedback: This is the booth mistake again. It leaves out the demo time that helped close many of those deals.

options.text: $80: ads plus sales time, divided by 400
options.feedback: Much closer. But the free month cost $4,000 in revenue you gave up to win these users.

options.text: $90: ads, sales time and the free month, divided by 400
options.feedback: $36,000 ÷ 400 = $90. Every cost of winning these users, divided by users who actually pay.

cards.title: Count everything it took to win them.
body: The cost to win a customer is every dollar and hour spent to bring them in, divided by the customers who actually signed. The invoice is only the start.
**Try it today:** pick your main way of finding customers. List every cost behind it, including people's time, and divide by last month's new customers.
